scenes.line1: Can you trust a small sample?
scenes.say: If you only analyze part of your data, how can you be sure your results are reliable?

scenes.label: Sampling
scenes.sub: Pick a subset to estimate the whole population.
scenes.say: Sampling means selecting a smaller group from a larger population to make predictions or estimates.
No matter how messy the original data is, the average of many samples starts to look normal, thanks to the central limit theorem.

scenes.title: Draw 100 samples from skewed data
scenes.say: When you repeat sampling, those sample averages pile up into a bell curve, even if the original data is skewed.

scenes.question: Why does the central limit theorem matter?
scenes.wrong: It only works for normal populations.
scenes.right: It lets us use normal-based inference for any population if the sample is large enough.
scenes.say: Don’t get tripped up—this theorem works even if your population isn’t normal. That’s key for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.
